business_patterns.top_pattern: CA HMO acute hospital spend is concentrated at UCI Medical Center
key_driver_codes: Esophagitis, Gastroenteritis and Miscellaneous Digestive Disorders with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: The largest cost increase is a CA HMO acute hospital pattern that is overwhelmingly concentrated at UCI Medical Center rather than spread broadly across hospitals. Both claim volume and paid per case increased, and a smaller chest pain utilization signal adds to the pressure. This points to a provider-specific inpatient cost issue with both network and utilization levers.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A single-provider concentration creates a direct opportunity to address the biggest dollar trend through contracting, reimbursement, and inpatient management action.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Launch a joint network and UM review of UCI Medical Center HMO acute admissions, including contract terms, admission management, and case management for chest pain and digestive admissions.
evidence_summary: CA HMO acute hospital spend increased about $5.1M.
About 95% of that increase was concentrated at UCI Medical Center.
UCI Medical Center showed about 236 more claims and about $20K higher paid per admission.
A smaller chest pain utilization increase added about $16K.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA rare high-cost inpatient Med/Surg cases are driving a focused outlier pattern
key_driver_codes: Pathological Fractures and Musculoskeletal and Connective Tissue Malignancy with MCC
Cardiac Valve and Other Major Cardiothoracic Procedures without Cardiac Catheterization with CC
Esophagitis, Gastroenteritis and Miscellaneous Digestive Disorders without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA inpatient Med/Surg cost growth is being driven by a very small number of exceptionally expensive admissions, largely at UCI Medical Center. The pattern is not broad utilization growth; it is a rare-case severity and payment issue concentrated in a few claims. These cases need targeted clinical and payment review rather than broad utilization controls.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A handful of catastrophic inpatient cases can materially move results and require different action than routine admission growth.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Perform a case-level clinical and claims audit on the few CA IP Med/Surg outlier admissions to confirm severity, coding completeness, and payment treatment before making broader policy changes.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The increase is concentrated in a few single-admission outliers with very high paid amounts and blank procedure fields, so claim and coding validation is required before broader action.
evidence_summary: CA IP Med/Surg rare-case spend increased about $0.9M.
Three single-admission cases drove most of the change at about $268K, $261K, and $256K.
Each driver came from one claim with very high paid per admission, indicating rare catastrophic cases rather than broad utilization growth.

business_patterns.top_pattern: NY EPO results are being moved by a single appendix admission
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: NY EPO / ACUTE HOSPITAL / IP Med/Surg
business_patterns.pattern_details: The NY signal is centered on a single appendix admission that shows up in both the acute hospital and clinical views. This is a one-case emergence, not a broad product or hospital trend. Action should focus on validating the claim and determining whether it represents appropriate severity, routing, and reimbursement.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Single-case events can look material in small segments, but they should not drive policy or network changes until validated.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Validate the full claim pathway for the NY appendix admission and, if accurate, treat it as a one-off surgical event rather than a broad EPO cost trend.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Both the operational and clinical patterns are fully concentrated in one low-baseline case.
evidence_summary: NY spend increased about $0.2M when the same appendix admission appeared in both acute hospital and clinical views.
The identified case added 1 claim and about $100K paid per admission.
The full signal is concentrated in Appendix Procedures with CC tied to diagnosis K3532.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA PPO maternity delivery costs show a small but focused severity and pricing issue
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA PPO / ACUTE HOSPITAL / IP OB Dlvry/Well NB
key_driver_codes: Vaginal Delivery without Sterilization or D&C with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA PPO maternity-related cost growth is concentrated in a narrow delivery pattern rather than broad maternity volume. The clinical view shows a small number of higher-cost vaginal delivery cases tied to O480, while the operational view shows unit-cost pressure without claim growth. This points to severity and reimbursement review for a focused delivery subtype.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Maternity episodes require different clinical and payment actions than general inpatient trends, even when the dollar impact is modest.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review the PPO maternity delivery claims for clinical severity and payment terms, focusing on vaginal delivery with MCC and whether reimbursement is exceeding expected delivery complexity.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is driven by a very small number of maternity cases, so case validation is needed before scaling any maternity policy response.
evidence_summary: CA PPO maternity-related spend increased about $46K.
Clinical review shows 2 higher-cost vaginal delivery cases tied to O480, adding about $27K.
Operational acute hospital pricing added about $19K with no claim growth, indicating unit-cost pressure rather than broad volume growth.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA PPO ancillary and lab spend is obscured by Not Mapped classification
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA PPO / Not Mapped ancillary and lab claims
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA PPO ancillary and lab cost growth is appearing in Not Mapped buckets across both operational and clinical views, with concentration in BillionToOne, Labcorp, and Virtual Radiologic claims. The same pattern also appears in outpatient lab and misc management categories with prenatal and screening-related diagnoses. Because both service classification and facility mapping are unclear, this is a validation-first issue before any UM, reimbursement, or network action.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Unmapped claims can create false provider-mix and utilization signals, leading to the wrong business action if classification is not corrected first.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a focused mapping audit for CA PPO claims from BillionToOne, Labcorp, and Virtual Radiologic that are landing in Not Mapped facility or DRG buckets, then reassess whether any UM or payment action is still warranted after the data are corrected.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Multiple groups carry unmapped or unknown classification flags across operational and clinical views, so the true service setting and claim type must be confirmed first.
evidence_summary: CA PPO Not Mapped ancillary and lab claims added about $83K across operational and clinical views.
BillionToOne Laboratory drove about $31K operationally, while Labcorp added about $7K and Virtual Radiologic added about $2K.
Clinical Not Mapped outpatient lab and misc management buckets added about $19K and $16K, largely tied to pathology and laboratory services.
Several drivers carry unmapped classification flags, so the current categorization may be obscuring the true site of care and service type.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA PPO acute hospital inpatient costs are rising in isolated low-volume cases
key_driver_codes: Esophagitis, Gastroenteritis and Miscellaneous Digestive Disorders with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Outside the maternity pattern, CA PPO acute hospital change is limited to a few one-claim inpatient cases in chest pain and digestive DRGs. The dollars are small, but each case carries meaningful paid-per-admission impact. This looks like isolated inpatient case emergence rather than a broad acute hospital trend.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Small low-volume inpatient spikes can be overread as trend unless they are separated from broader pricing or utilization issues.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review the small set of CA PPO acute inpatient claims for chest pain and digestive admissions to confirm level of care and payment accuracy, and avoid broader action unless the pattern repeats.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The increase is driven by a few low-baseline, one-claim cases.
evidence_summary: CA PPO acute hospital inpatient spend increased about $16K.
The main drivers were one digestive case at about $8K and one chest pain case at about $8K.
Both drivers are low-volume and concentrated in single claims, with paid per admission carrying the increase.

business_patterns.top_pattern: NH HMO shows a small unmapped radiology utilization uptick
business_patterns.pattern_details: NH HMO has a small-dollar increase concentrated in Virtual Radiologic Professionals claims that are classified as Not Mapped. The claim count increase suggests more activity, but the unmapped setting makes it unclear whether this is real utilization growth or a routing change. This should be handled as a targeted validation item, not a broad trend.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Even small-dollar changes can point to emerging provider-routing or classification issues that recur later if not corrected.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Verify whether the NH HMO Virtual Radiologic claim increase reflects true utilization or a mapping change, and correct provider or facility classification if needed.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The signal is low baseline, low dollar, and sits in a Not Mapped classification.
evidence_summary: NH HMO Not Mapped spend increased about $4K.
Virtual Radiologic Professionals accounted for the signal with about 34 more claims.
The dollar impact is small, but the unmapped classification makes the cause uncertain.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CO and MO have small-dollar unmapped ancillary claim emergence
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CO EPO and MO PPO / Not Mapped
business_patterns.pattern_details: CO and MO each show very small unmapped ancillary claim increases with low baseline activity. One is centered on a single Labcorp EPO claim in CO, and the other on Virtual Radiologic PPO claims in MO. These are best treated as low-priority validation items unless they recur.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Low-dollar unmapped claim emergence can distract teams if it is mistaken for a broader operational or provider trend.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Triage the CO and MO Not Mapped ancillary claims as data-quality validation items, confirm provider classification, and defer broader policy action unless repeat activity appears.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Both signals are low baseline, low dollar, and flagged as unmapped, limiting confidence in broader business interpretation.
evidence_summary: CO and MO Not Mapped ancillary claims added about $5K combined.
CO EPO Labcorp contributed about $3K from a single low-baseline claim.
MO PPO Virtual Radiologic contributed about $2K with about 24 more claims.
Both signals are flagged as low baseline and unmapped, limiting confidence in operational conclusions.

executive_summary.headline: Most of the cost change is concentrated in CA acute hospital business at UCI Medical Center, while the remaining themes are mainly rare inpatient outliers and unmapped ancillary claims that require validation before policy action.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: The dominant business story is a CA HMO acute hospital increase centered on one provider, UCI Medical Center, with both higher volume and higher paid per case. Secondary patterns split into two very different actions: targeted review of rare high-cost inpatient cases, and correction of Not Mapped ancillary and lab claims that currently blur provider-mix and utilization signals. Maternity and NY appendix activity are present, but they are focused low-volume patterns rather than broad trend shifts.
recommended_focus_order: CA HMO acute hospital concentration at UCI Medical Center
CA rare high-cost IP Med/Surg outliers and the NY appendix one-off case
CA PPO Not Mapped ancillary and lab mapping cleanup before broader UM or reimbursement action

notes: All 15 analytical groups were assigned to a business pattern.
The NY operational and clinical appendix groups were merged into one low-baseline emergence pattern because they describe the same one-case business event.
CA operational and clinical Not Mapped lab and ancillary groups were consolidated into one gating validation pattern.
CO and MO low-dollar Not Mapped groups were combined because they share the same low-baseline validation mechanism and are individually immaterial.
